newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, Waigel reject talk of EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, Waigel reject talk of EMU delay.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday dismissed talk about delaying the euro after the Bundesbank hinted the currency might be delayed if big countries did not qualify for it.

Bonn's drive to launch Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 got a boost from Germany's six leading economic institutes, which said they believed Bonn could still meet the tough deficit target needed to join the club.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who also assumes the single currency will start on time, sparked off talk of delay by commenting on Monday evening that the project might have to be put off if big countries failed to clear the entry bar.
Another Bundesbank council member, Franz-Christoph Zeitler, expressed confidence Germany could have its budget deficit meet the target of three percent of gross domestic product.
"We will have the euro on time," Kohl said in a speech in Bonn. "We Germans will keep to the criteria."
Waigel, commenting on the institutes' semi-annual report on the German economy, said: "We will hold to the criteria, they will not be loosened ... We will make it."

Tietmeyer mentioned a possible EMU delay at a bankers' meeting in Guetersloh after he said the currency union would do best if it were led by a homogeneous group of states. He did not say which countries should be part of the first wave.
But he added: "If it is the case that the big countries fail to meet the criteria, then a delay could be considered."
If this became clear, then "it would be better to say so sooner (rather than later)," he added.
In the Netherlands, which holds the current EU presidency, both Prime Minister Wim Kok and central bank president Wim Duisenberg said EMU could not start without Germany and France.
"European Monetary Union without (either or both) is a non-starter," Kok stressed.

Quizzed by journalists in Munich, Zeitler shied away from such clarity but insisted the EMU criteria must not be softened and added: "The foundation of a house is more important than the moving-in date."
Zeitler said President Jacques Chirac's decision to call snap parliamentary elections showed France's commitment to EMU.
The economic institutes said Bonn had a chance to make a "point landing" on its budget deficit to qualify for EMU but urged quick action to reform and consolidate state finances.
The independent forecasters saw overall GDP growth rising to just 2.25 percent this year and 2.75 percent in 1998, a slower rate of recovery than the government is hoping for.

They still expected European monetary union (EMU) to start on time with a large number of countries, including Germany, but the starting roster would be a political decision that cannot be reduced to simple arithmetic targets.
"We expect a deficit of 3.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, falling to 2.9 percent in 1998," said economist Willi Leibfritz of the Ifo institute, speaking for the group.
"But 3.0 percent is still thoroughly possible (in 1997)."
The forecast is a slight improvement from the institutes' fall prognosis of a 1997 deficit equal to 3.5 percent of GDP.

The institutes also said they expected Bonn's outstanding debt to exceed the 60 percent of GDP Maastricht guideline, but it would probably plead that the costs of German unification are a "special factor" that should be considered.
"The decision will be a judgment of whether policies are sound and sustainable over the long-term," Leibfritz said. "It will not be a question of pure numbers."
